samples.text:
The graph shows the percentage of paper, glass, aluminium cans and plastic that was recycled in a city from 2000 to 2020.

Paper had the highest recycling rate in every year. In 2000 it was 45% and it increased to 58% in 2005 and 66% in 2010. After that it grew more slowly and it was 72% in 2020. Glass was the second. It started at 30% and went up steadily to 55% in 2010 and 68% in 2020, so it was nearly same as paper at the end.

The recycling of aluminium cans was 20% in 2000. It increased quickly to 52% in 2010 and 60% in 2015, but then it drop a little to 58% in 2020. This was the only material which decreased.

Plastic had the lowest rate in all the years. In 2000 only 3% of plastic were recycled. It increased slowly to 14% in 2010 and then it rise to 30% in 2020.

Overall, the recycling rates of all materials was higher in 2020 than in 2000, and paper was the highest while plastic was the lowest.
samples.why: Overview present but placed at the end · key features covered, including the aluminium dip · repetitive sentence patterns · agreement, article and verb form errors that do not affect meaning.

samples.text:
The line graph illustrates how the recycling rates for four materials, paper, glass, aluminium cans and plastic, changed in a city over a twenty-year period from 2000.

Overall, the proportion of each material being recycled increased considerably. Paper was recycled at the highest rate throughout, whereas plastic consistently had the lowest rate, despite showing steady growth.

In 2000, 45% of paper was recycled, and this figure rose quickly to 66% in 2010 before levelling off at 72% in 2020. Glass followed a similar upward trend but from a lower starting point of 30%. Its rate increased steadily, reaching 68% by the end of the period, only four points below paper.

Aluminium cans saw the most rapid improvement in the first decade, with the rate increasing from 20% to 52%. It peaked at 60% in 2015 but then slightly declined to 58% in 2020, making it the only material whose recycling rate fell at any point. Plastic, on the other hand, was recycled at very low levels, with only 3% in 2000. Nevertheless, its rate grew continuously, reaching 30% by 2020, which was ten times its initial figure.
samples.why: Clear overview · key features and the aluminium decline highlighted · logical grouping · good use of derived comparisons · appropriate vocabulary · mostly accurate grammar with a minor word order slip.

samples.text:
The graph compares the percentage of paper, glass, aluminium cans and plastic recycled in a city at five-year intervals between 2000 and 2020.

Overall, recycling rates improved for all four materials over the two decades. Paper was recycled most extensively throughout, while plastic lagged well behind the others, although it recorded the largest relative increase.

Paper began the period with a recycling rate of 45%, which rose quickly to 66% in 2010 and then more slowly to 72% in 2020. Glass showed a comparable but steeper trajectory, more than doubling from 30% to 68%, so that by the end of the period it had almost caught up with paper.

Aluminium cans registered the sharpest gains in the first decade, with their recycling rate soaring from 20% to 52%. Growth then slowed, and after peaking at 60% in 2015 the rate dipped marginally to 58%, the only decline shown on the graph. Plastic, by contrast, started from a strikingly low base of just 3%. Its rate rose gradually but consistently, reaching 30% in 2020; while this represented a tenfold increase, it was still only around half the rate for aluminium cans, the next lowest material.
samples.why: Key features skilfully selected, including relative versus absolute change · clear overview · accurate figures and derived comparisons · precise, varied vocabulary · wide range of error-free structures.
